newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian defence minister rejects talk of mutiny.
newsitem.headline: Russian defence minister rejects talk of mutiny.

text.p: Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov admitted on Saturday the financially-strapped armed forces were in trouble but attacked critics who have suggested some units might mutiny.

Although he did not mention anyone by name, it seemed clear Rodionov's words were aimed at former security supremo Alexander Lebed, who on Thursday said problems in the military would lead to a "hot autumn".

"The situation in the armed forces is rather complicated, first of all because of lack of normal financing. But regardless of this, the situation is fully under control and manageable," Rodionov told Russian television.
He called on the country's politicians to pull together to preserve order in the armed forces and criticised those who he said were speaking out of turn.
"With such careless acts they cause colossal damage, especially by misleading the public," he said.

"It's a great shame that some politicians do not understand that in the difficult conditions in which the country and the armed forces find themselves, unpopular measures may be needed to stabilise the situation and improve it."
Lebed, sacked by President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday for causing waves in the Kremlin, enjoys great support among the rank and file of the armed forces.

At a news conference held hours after his sacking, he cited a letter from a group of General Staff officers in which they told the Defence Ministry to pay all salary arrears by October 25 or face the consequences.

Lebed, a former paratroop general, opposes what he says are plans to cripple the airborne forces by slashing their numbers by a third. The deputy chief of airborne troops was sacked on Thursday for opposing Rodionov's decision to cut his force.

"We are not going to liquidate the airborne troops. By cutting them down a bit, we aim to improve their quality. Why do we need a large number of paratroop divisions when they are not up to strength and lack modern weapons?" Rodionov said.
"We will have two divisions but they will be up to strength and they will have modern weapons and training facilities."
Lebed's sacking removed another thorn from the flesh of Rodionov, who has gradually been replacing the Defence Ministry's old guard with his own men.

Armed forces chief of staff Mikhail Kolesnikov was sacked on Friday but Rodionov said this had nothing to do with Lebed. Instead, he said, Kolesnikov has been removed to freshen up the work of the general staff.

"When a man works for a long time at the same job, he loses the sharpness of his senses, the perception of what's happening around him. Putting it in a rather crude way, rust and barnacles build up and have be cleaned off," he said.
